chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from Abdullah ibn Aamir from Ali ibn Mahziyar from Ali ibn Ismail al-Mithammi from Rabi' ibn Abdullah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said:

Indeed, patience and affliction race to the Believer, so the affliction comes to him while he is patient; and indeed, panic and affliction race to the Infidel, so the affliction comes to him while he is panicking.

key_terms.الصَّبْرُ: Patience, perseverance in the face of hardship
key_terms.الْجَزَعُ: Panic, restlessness, anxiety in the face of hardship
key_terms.يَسْتَبِقَانِ: They race each other, compete to arrive first

ai.seo_question: How does the reaction to affliction differ between a believer and a disbeliever in Shia theology?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the dynamic interplay between internal spiritual disposition and external trials, highlighting how the believer's inherent patience (sabr) transforms affliction into a means of elevation, whereas the disbeliever's innate restlessness (jaz') exacerbates suffering. Rooted in the chapter on patience, it reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on the believer's active spiritual readiness, where the 'race' between trial and temperament determines the quality of one's endurance. This concept underscores the theological view that suffering is not merely punitive but revelatory of one's inner state.
